content: Urinary incontinence is a widespread and debilitating condition that affects approximately 50% of women at some point in their lives. Among these cases, stress urinary incontinence (SUI) is a leading cause, affecting 30% to 80% of women with incontinence. This condition imposes a significant health and economic burden on both the affected individuals and society. Mid-urethral sling (MUS) operations are a well-established, minimally invasive surgical treatment for SUI. The procedure involves placing a small strip of tape through either the retropubic or obturator space, with entry or exit points located at the lower abdomen or groin, respectively. This review does not include single-incision slings. The objective of this review was to evaluate the clinical outcomes of MUS procedures in women with SUI, urodynamic stress incontinence (USI), or mixed urinary incontinence (MUI). The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials in which both trial arms involved MUS operations. A total of 81 trials, encompassing 12,113 women, were included in the analysis. The quality of evidence for most outcomes was assessed as moderate, primarily due to risks of bias or imprecision. When comparing the transobturator route (TOR) and the retropubic route (RPR), data from 55 trials involving 8,652 women showed that the short-term (up to one year) subjective cure rates were similar between the two approaches. Subjective cure rates ranged from 62% to 98% in the TOR group and from 71% to 97% in the RPR group. Objective cure rates in the short term were also comparable between the two groups. Medium-term (one to five years) and long-term (over five years) data were more limited, but subjective cure rates remained similar between the groups. In the long term, subjective cure rates ranged from 43% to 92% in the TOR group and from 51% to 88% in the RPR group. The RPR approach was associated with higher morbidity compared to TOR, although the overall rate of adverse events was low. Bladder perforation occurred less frequently with TOR (0.6% versus 4.5%). Other complications, such as major vascular or visceral injury, longer operating times, greater blood loss, and longer hospital stays, were also less common with TOR. Postoperative voiding dysfunction was less frequent following TOR, but groin pain was more common in the TOR group (6.4% versus 1.3%). Conversely, suprapubic pain was less frequent in the TOR group (0.8% versus 2.9%). Both types of pain were generally short-lived. Vaginal tape erosion, exposure, or extrusion occurred at low rates in both groups, with 24 instances per 1,000 women in the TOR group and 21 per 1,000 in the RPR group. Limited data were available regarding the need for repeat incontinence surgery in the long term, but the likelihood of requiring additional surgery was higher in the TOR group compared to the RPR group. Among retropubic approaches, the bottom-to-top route was more effective than the top-to-bottom route for achieving subjective cure. This approach also resulted in fewer cases of voiding dysfunction, bladder perforations, and vaginal tape erosions. When comparing transobturator techniques, the medial-to-lateral and lateral-to-medial approaches showed similar shortand medium-term subjective cure rates. However, voiding dysfunction was more frequent in the medial-to-lateral group, while vaginal perforation was less common. Due to the very low quality of evidence, it remains unclear whether the lower rates of vaginal perforation in the medial-to-lateral group influenced the risk of vaginal tape erosion. In conclusion, mid-urethral sling operations are the most extensively studied surgical treatment for SUI in women and have demonstrated a favorable safety profile. Regardless of the surgical route, MUS procedures are highly effective in the short and medium term, with accumulating evidence supporting their long-term efficacy. These procedures significantly improve the quality of life for women with SUI. A brief economic analysis suggested that the transobturator approach may be more cost-effective than the retropubic approach. While fewer adverse events were associated with the transobturator route, groin pain was more common. Among retropubic techniques, the bottom-to-top route was superior to the top-to-bottom route. The review highlights the need for longer-term outcome data from existing trials to address uncertainties regarding long-term effectiveness and adverse event profiles.
